newsitem.title: PERU: Dominican Republic offers asylum to Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Dominican Republic offers asylum to Peru rebels.

text.p: The Dominican Republic offered asylum on Friday to some of the Peruvian guerrillas holding 72 hostages, but the rebels gave no sign they would accept the offer or ease their demands for releasing their captives.

A Dominican government statement said President Leonel Fernandez accepted a request from visiting Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to take in some of the rebels occupying the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru since Dec. 17.
"The government expressed its agreement to receive some of the rebels in Lima" as a way of contributing to a peaceful resolution of the crisis, the statement said.

Komura thanked the Dominican Republic and Cuba, which also agreed to take in Peruvian guerrillas if there was a negotiated settlement of the three-month hostage siege, but he was not optimistic that would happen soon.

"There is still some distance between the Peruvian government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA)," the Japanese official told a news conference in Santo Domingo. "We should not be too optimistic."

Komura on Thursday won confirmation from Cuba that it would accept some of the 20-odd rebels who have been holding the hostages at the Japanese mansion. Despite the asylum offers, the MRTA rebels say they do not want asylum abroad, preferring to return to their jungle strongholds after the siege. But they have apparently not ruled out asylum and they kept silent on Thursday.

On the rebels' main demand of freedom for more than 400 captured comrades, negotiations appeared to be going nowhere. President Alberto Fujimori nixed any chance of a deal to release the prisoners, saying Peruvians had endured too many years of guerrilla violence and too many deaths to allow any such deal.
"I absolutely, totally and flatly deny that my government's position has changed," Fujimori said on Thursday. "There will be no freeing of MRTA prisoners.

"The security of the country comes before any other interest. I'm sorry if that sounds hard," he said in response to media reports that he had told the Japanese envoy he would release some prisoners to help speed up a solution.

"Perhaps for other countries this might not have so much meaning and they may seek solutions that don't take this into account, but we Peruvians have suffered for 15 years and we've had 25,000 deaths," Fujimori said.

Despite his tough stand, there were signs of movement toward a solution in some peripheral areas. A group of doctors who have been checking on the hostages' health visited a women's jail in Lima where about 300 people are held under anti-terrorism laws.

Their mission at Chorrillos jail was not known, but given that Fujimori has been reported ready to improve prison conditions as a concession to the hostage-takers, the visit added to speculation that progress was being made on that front.

A group of MRTA women prisoners have been on hunger strike to demand that visiting days be restored. The hostage-takers have demanded independent reports on the health of the hunger strikers, suggesting that may be part of the doctors' mission.

The hostages have spent Christmas and New Year's under the guns of their captors, and a Red Cross statement suggested they may be there for Easter too. The statement asked relatives to send clean clothes, books and any other items, and collect their dirty laundry, on Friday, March 28, two days before Easter.

The MRTA met Thursday in the besieged home with two members of a mediation panel overseeing talks with the government -- Red Cross representative Michel Minnig and Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent. Another meeting was expected Friday, a rebel source said by radio from the residence.
The government has said it will use force only if the hostages are harmed but is known to be training crack troops around a mock-up of the compound in case of an assault.
